title: Nedd4l combined scores
shortDescription: Model combined scores for E3 ubiquitin-protein ligase NEDD4-like.

experiment.title: Nedd4l combined scores
experiment.shortDescription: Model combined scores for E3 ubiquitin-protein ligase NEDD4-like.
experiment.abstractText: This study measured the digestion of E3 ubiquitin-protein ligase NEDD4-like protein variants with both trypsin and chymotripsin to measure the effect of these variants on folding. The target accession used in the original study is 1WR7.pdb.
experiment.methodText: The score column is the dG value calculated using the coupled model, calculated from the counts across replicates and proteases. dG values were fit directly using a Bayesian model, assuming that each sequence has a shared dG value that is shared across both proteases. Removed 1 duplicated variant.

title: Nedd4l trypsin digestion
shortDescription: Trypsin digestion of E3 ubiquitin-protein ligase NEDD4-like.

experiment.title: Nedd4l trypsin digestion
experiment.shortDescription: Trypsin digestion of E3 ubiquitin-protein ligase NEDD4-like.
experiment.abstractText: This study measured the digestion of E3 ubiquitin-protein ligase NEDD4-like protein variants with trypsin to measure the effect of these variants on folding. The target accession used in the original study is 1WR7.pdb.
experiment.methodText: Sequences were reverse-transcribed and codon optimized using E. coli codon frequencies. Oligo libraries containing mutations were purchased from Agilent or Twist. The libraries were transcribed and translated using cDNA display such that proteins are attached to the cDNA at the C-terminus and have a PA tag at the N-terminus. The protein-cDNA complexes were purified and subjected to a protease assay such that only undigested molecules would retain the PA tag and the cDNA linkage. High-throughput Illumina sequencing was used to quantify the amount of each variant after the assay.

title: NEDD4L WW domain domainome 1.0
shortDescription: Stability measurements of the NEDD4L WW domain from domainome 1.0.

experiment.title: NEDD4L WW domain from domainome 1.0
experiment.shortDescription: Stability measurements of the NEDD4L WW domain from domainome 1.0.
experiment.abstractText: This study measured the stability of the WW domain in NEDD4L using a DHFR protein-fragment complementation assay that couples the cellular abundance of the target protein expressed in yeast to yeast growth. The identifier used in the original study is Q96PU5_PF00397_184.
experiment.methodText: Oligonucleotide libraries encoding the domains were generated using mMPS synthesis technology (BGI). Variant domain sequences were fused to a fragment of an essential gene (DHFR) and transformed into yeast cells. Unstable domains are degraded by the cell, reducing DHFR fragment concentration and impeding cell growth in the presence of methotrexate. A total of 27 selections (3 replicates each of 9 sub-libraries) were performed. Variant frequencies before and after cell growth were measured by high-throughput sequencing of amplicon libraries containing the mutated domains. Fitness associated with each variant and their errors were derived using DiMSum v1.2.11 (Faure et al., 2020).

primaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: Site saturation mutagenesis of 500 human protein domains reveals the contribution of protein destabilization to genetic disease
primaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: Missense variants that change the amino acid sequences of proteins cause one third of human genetic diseases1. Tens of millions of missense variants exist in the current human population, with the vast majority having unknown functional consequences. Here we present the first large-scale experimental analysis of human missense variants across many different proteins. Using DNA synthesis and cellular selection experiments we quantify the impact of >500,000 variants on the abundance of >500 human protein domains. This dataset - Human Domainome 1.0 - reveals that >60% of pathogenic missense variants reduce protein stability. The contribution of stability to protein fitness varies across proteins and diseases, and is particularly important in recessive disorders. We show how stability measurements can be combined with protein language models to annotate functional sites and that measurements made on a small number of proteins can be used to accurately predict stability changes across entire protein families using energy models. Domainome 1.0 demonstrates the feasibility of assaying human protein variants at scale and provides a large consistent reference dataset for clinical variant interpretation and the training and benchmarking of computational methods.
